sourceSentences.text: ‘It is, of course, quite lovely,’ one Lady Hope ventured to say.
‘But very cold.
And there is little that can be done here until the snow melts and the wind grows kinder.’
‘Oh, but you are wrong!’
Queen Kettricken exclaimed.
She laughed aloud as she straightened up from her treasures, walked again to the centre of the tower top.
‘A garden begins in the heart.
I must sweep the snow and ice from the tower top tomorrow.
And then, all these benches and statues and pots must be set out.
But how?
Like the spokes of a wheel?
As a charming maze?
Formally, by variation of height and theme?
There are a thousand ways they could be arranged, and I must experiment.
Unless, perhaps, my lord will remember it for me just as it once was.
Then I shall restore it to him, the garden of his childhood!’
‘Tomorrow, Queen Kettricken.
For the skies grow dark, and colder,’ advised Lady Modesty.
I could see what the climb followed by standing in the cold had cost the older woman.
But she smiled kindly as she spoke.
‘I could, perhaps, tell you tonight what I remember of this garden.’
‘Would you?’
Kettricken exclaimed, and clasped both of her hands in her own.
The smile she shed on Lady Modesty was like a blessing.
‘I should be glad to.’
And on those words we slowly began to file from the rooftop.
I was the last to go.
I pulled the door closed behind me and stood for a moment letting my eyes adjust to the darkness in the tower.
Below me, candles bobbed as the others descended.
I blessed whatever page had thought to run and fetch them.
I followed more slowly, my whole arm, from bite to sword cut, throbbing nastily.
I thought of Kettricken’s joy, and was glad of it, even as I guiltily reflected that it was built on a false foundation.
Verity had been relieved at my suggestion to turn the garden over to Kettricken, but the act had not the significance to him that it did to Kettricken.
She would attack this project as if she were building a shrine to their love.
I doubted that by the morrow Verity would even recall he had gifted her with it.
I felt both traitorous and foolish as I descended the steps.
I went to the evening meal thinking I wished to be alone, so I avoided the hall, and took myself instead to the guardroom off the kitchen.
There I encountered both Burrich and Hands at their meal.
When they invited me to join them, I could not refuse.
But once I was seated, it was as if I were not there.
They did not exclude me from their conversation but they spoke of a life I no longer shared.
The immensely rich detail of all that went on in the stables and mews eluded me now.
They discussed problems with the confident briskness of men who shared an intimate background knowledge.
More and more, I found myself nodding at their words, but contributing nothing.
They got along well.
Burrich did not speak down to Hands.
But Hands did not conceal his respect for a man he clearly regarded as his superior.
Hands had learned much from Burrich in a short time.
He had left Buckkeep as a lowly stable-boy last autumn.
He now spoke competently of the hawks and dogs and asked solid questions concerning Burrich’s breeding choices for the horses.
I was still eating when they got up to leave.
Hands was concerned about a dog that had been kicked by a horse earlier in the day.
They wished me good evening, and continued to talk together as they went out the door.
I sat quietly.
There were others about me, guards and soldiers, eating and drinking and talking.
The pleasant sounds of talk, of spoon against the pot’s side, the thud as someone cut a wedge of cheese from a wheel was like a music.
The room smelled of food and folk, of the wood fire and spilled ale and the rich stew bubbling.
I should have felt content, not restless.
Nor melancholy.
Not alone.

Они обсуждали проблемы с уверенной деловитостью людей, разделяющих глубокое общее знание.
Всё чаще я ловил себя на том, что киваю их словам, но ничего не добавляю.
Они хорошо ладили.
Баррич не говорил с Хэндсом свысока.
Но Хэндс и не скрывал уважения к человеку, которого явно считал выше себя.

Прошлой осенью он покинул Баккип простым конюшенным мальчишкой.
Теперь он со знанием дела говорил о соколах и собаках и задавал толковые вопросы о выборе Баррича при разведении лошадей.
Я всё ещё ел, когда они поднялись уходить.
Хэндса беспокоила собака, которую раньше в тот день лягнула лошадь.
Они пожелали мне доброго вечера и продолжали разговаривать, выходя за дверь.
Я сидел тихо.

Приятные звуки разговора, ложки о край котла, глухой удар, когда кто-то отрезал клин сыра от круглой головки, были словно музыка.

Я должен был бы чувствовать довольство, а не беспокойство.
И не тоску.
И не одиночество.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: And on those words we slowly began to file from the rooftop. I was the last to go. I pulled the door closed behind me and stood for a moment letting my eyes adjust to the darkness in the tower. Below me, candles bobbed as the others descended. I blessed whatever page had thought to run and fetch them. I followed more slowly, my whole arm, from bite to sword cut, throbbing nastily. I thought of Kettricken’s joy, and was glad of it, even as I guiltily reflected that it was built on a false foundation. Verity had been relieved at my suggestion to turn the garden over to Kettricken, but the act had not the significance to him that it did to Kettricken. She would attack this project as if she were building a shrine to their love. I doubted that by the morrow Verity would even recall he had gifted her with it. I felt both traitorous and foolish as I descended the steps.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: И с этими словами мы медленно потянулись с крыши. Я уходил последним. Я притворил за собой дверь и на миг остановился, давая глазам привыкнуть к темноте башни. Внизу покачивались огоньки свечей — остальные спускались. Я благословил того пажа, которому пришло в голову сбегать за ними. Я шёл медленнее; вся моя рука, от укуса до раны от меча, мучительно пульсировала. Я думал о радости Кетриккен и радовался ей, хотя с чувством вины понимал, что она покоится на ложном основании. Верити обрадовался моему предложению отдать сад Кетриккен, но для него этот поступок не имел того значения, какое придавала ему Кетриккен. Она возьмётся за это дело так, словно возводит святилище их любви. Я сомневался, что к завтрашнему дню Верити вообще вспомнит, что подарил ей этот сад. Спускаясь по ступеням, я чувствовал себя и предателем, и глупцом.

paragraphPairs.sourceText: I went to the evening meal thinking I wished to be alone, so I avoided the hall, and took myself instead to the guardroom off the kitchen. There I encountered both Burrich and Hands at their meal. When they invited me to join them, I could not refuse. But once I was seated, it was as if I were not there. They did not exclude me from their conversation but they spoke of a life I no longer shared. The immensely rich detail of all that went on in the stables and mews eluded me now. They discussed problems with the confident briskness of men who shared an intimate background knowledge. More and more, I found myself nodding at their words, but contributing nothing. They got along well. Burrich did not speak down to Hands. But Hands did not conceal his respect for a man he clearly regarded as his superior. Hands had learned much from Burrich in a short time. He had left Buckkeep as a lowly stable-boy last autumn. He now spoke competently of the hawks and dogs and asked solid questions concerning Burrich’s breeding choices for the horses. I was still eating when they got up to leave. Hands was concerned about a dog that had been kicked by a horse earlier in the day. They wished me good evening, and continued to talk together as they went out the door.
paragraphPairs.translatedText: На вечернюю трапезу я шёл с мыслью, что хочу побыть один, поэтому избегал зала и вместо этого направился в караульную у кухни. Там я застал за едой и Баррича, и Хэндса. Когда они пригласили меня присоединиться, я не мог отказаться. Но стоило мне сесть, как будто меня там и не было. Они не исключали меня из разговора, но говорили о жизни, которой я больше не разделял. Необъятное богатство подробностей всего, что происходило в конюшнях и соколятнях, теперь ускользало от меня.
